questions.hint: Shape is always (rows, columns). Count the inner lists first, then the numbers inside one list.
questions.explain: A has 2 rows (2 inner lists) and 3 columns (3 numbers in each row), so A.shape is (2, 3).

questions.hint: Python starts counting at 0. The first number picks the row, the second picks the column.
questions.explain: A[1, 2] = row 1 (the second row) and column 2 (the third column) = 60.

questions.q: What is np.dot(a, b)?
questions.code:
a = np.array([2, 3])
b = np.array([4, 5])
print(np.dot(a, b))
questions.hint: A dot product has two steps. Step 1 is the same as a * b. Step 2 turns the result into ONE number.
questions.explain: Multiply the pairs (2×4 = 8, 3×5 = 15), then add them: 8 + 15 = 23.

questions.q: A.shape is (2, 3) and B.shape is (3, 4). What is the shape of A @ B?
questions.hint: Write the shapes next to each other: (2, 3) @ (3, 4). The inside numbers must match. Which numbers are left?
questions.explain: (m, n) @ (n, p) → (m, p). Inside: 3 = 3, so it works. Outside numbers give the result: (2, 4).

questions.q: A.shape is (3, 4). Which array can NOT be added to A?
questions.hint: Read shapes from RIGHT to LEFT. Two sizes work together if they are equal, or if one of them is 1.
questions.explain: (3, 4) + (2,): the last sizes are 4 and 2. They are not equal and neither is 1, so it is an error. The other three all work.

questions.q: What does A.sum(axis=0) give?
questions.hint: axis=0 means move DOWN. You get one answer for every column.
questions.explain: axis=0 collapses the rows: 1+4 = 5, 2+5 = 7, 3+6 = 9 → [5 7 9]. axis=1 would give [6 15].

questions.q: What does print(data) show at the end?
questions.hint: np.delete builds something new. Did we keep it with an = sign?
questions.explain: np.delete returns a NEW array, but we did not save it. data is still [10 20 30 40]. To keep it: data = np.delete(data, 1).

questions.q: A neural-network layer: what is Y.shape?
questions.code:
X.shape  # (32, 10)  → 32 samples, 10 features
W.shape  # (10, 4)
b.shape  # (4,)
Y = X @ W + b
questions.hint: Do it in two steps. First use the shape rule for X @ W. Then ask: does + b change the shape?
questions.explain: (32, 10) @ (10, 4) → (32, 4). b with shape (4,) is broadcast to every row, so Y stays (32, 4).

questions.q: A student writes df["name", "math"] to get two columns. What happens?
options: pandas returns only the first column, name, and ignores math
pandas returns a table with the two columns name and math
pandas joins the two columns together into one text column
KeyError: pandas looks for ONE column called ("name", "math")
questions.hint: Look at the brackets. How many brackets do you need to give pandas a LIST of column names?
questions.explain: Two columns need a list inside the brackets: df[["name", "math"]]. With one bracket pandas searches for a single column with that strange name → KeyError.

questions.q: df has the normal index 0, 1, 2, … How many rows does df.loc[0:2] return?
questions.hint: loc uses labels (names), not positions. Does a slice with labels include the end, or stop before it?
questions.explain: loc includes the end label: 0, 1 and 2 → 3 rows. iloc[0:2] would stop before 2 → only 2 rows.

questions.q: How many rows does this filter return?
questions.code:
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Aziz", "Malika", "Bekzod", "Dilnoza",
             "Jasur", "Nilufar", "Sardor", "Kamola"],
    "city": ["Tashkent", "Samarkand", "Bukhara", "Tashkent",
             "Samarkand", "Tashkent", "Bukhara", "Samarkand"],
    "hours": [5, 8, 2, 6, 3, 7, 1, 4],
    "math": [85, 92, 60, 78, 70, 88, 55, np.nan],
    "english": [78, 88, 65, 90, np.nan, 84, 58, 75],
})

top = df[df["math"] >= 80]
print(len(top))
questions.hint: Check every math score one by one. What happens to a missing value (NaN) when you ask “is it ≥ 80?”
questions.explain: Only 85, 92 and 88 pass (Aziz, Malika, Nilufar). NaN ≥ 80 is False, so Kamola is dropped. → 3 rows.

questions.q: Which filter correctly finds students from Tashkent AND with math ≥ 80?
questions.hint: Check three things in each option: the AND sign pandas uses, the ( ) around each condition, and = versus ==.
questions.explain: pandas needs & (not and), ( ) around EACH condition, and == to compare. Only one option has all three.

questions.q: What does the last line print?
questions.code:
df["bonus"] = df["math"] + 5
df.drop(columns=["bonus"])
print("bonus" in df.columns)
questions.hint: Ask the key question from class: did df change, or did we just get a new result?
questions.explain: drop() returns a NEW table. We did not reassign, so bonus is still in df → True. Fix: df = df.drop(columns=["bonus"]).

questions.q: What is df["math"].mean()? (rounded)
questions.code:
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Aziz", "Malika", "Bekzod", "Dilnoza",
             "Jasur", "Nilufar", "Sardor", "Kamola"],
    "city": ["Tashkent", "Samarkand", "Bukhara", "Tashkent",
             "Samarkand", "Tashkent", "Bukhara", "Samarkand"],
    "hours": [5, 8, 2, 6, 3, 7, 1, 4],
    "math": [85, 92, 60, 78, 70, 88, 55, np.nan],
    "english": [78, 88, 65, 90, np.nan, 84, 58, 75],
})

# the 7 real math scores add up to 528
print(df["math"].mean())
questions.hint: Compare df["math"].count() with len(df). Which one does mean() divide by?
questions.explain: mean() skips NaN: 528 ÷ 7 = 75.43. It does NOT count the hole as 0 (528 ÷ 8 = 66.0 would be wrong).

questions.q: What value does this give for Bukhara?
questions.hint: Split first: find every Bukhara student's math score. Then apply mean() to only those scores.
questions.explain: Bukhara students: Bekzod 60 and Sardor 55. Mean = (60 + 55) ÷ 2 = 57.5.

questions.q: Which code answers: “Which city studies the most hours in total?”
questions.hint: Use the template WHO → WHAT → HOW. Who are the groups? Which column? Which summary?
questions.explain: WHO = city (the groups), WHAT = hours (the column), HOW = sum (total). count() would only count students.

questions.q: Question: “Did course sign-ups grow month by month this year?” Which chart is best?
questions.hint: Start from the question, not the chart. The key words are “month by month”.
questions.explain: Change over time → line chart. Histograms show spread, box plots compare spread, and pie charts are best avoided.

questions.q: In fig, ax = plt.subplots(), what is ax?
options: The legend box with the colours
One chart area inside the figure
questions.hint: Remember the confusing pair: axes is NOT the same as axis.
questions.explain: fig = the whole canvas. ax (axes) = one chart inside it. axis = one line (x or y).

questions.q: What does hue="time" do here?
options: Makes the dots bigger when the time is later
Colours each dot by the time column (Lunch / Dinner)
Puts the time column on the x-axis instead
Sorts the dots from the earliest to the latest time of day
questions.hint: x = across, y = up. hue adds a third column. How can a flat picture show a third column?
questions.explain: hue = colour by a column. Lunch and Dinner get different colours, and Seaborn makes the legend for you.

questions.q: In sns.barplot(data=tips, x="day", y="tip"), what is the height of each bar?
options: The biggest tip on that day
The total of all tips on that day
The average (mean) tip on that day
The number of bills on that day
questions.hint: Compare barplot with countplot from class. One shows “how many”. What does the other one show?
questions.explain: barplot height = the MEAN by default (for totals use estimator="sum"). countplot shows how many rows.
